tweets.text:
The market fundamentally misunderstands the role and functionality of open-weights models (MS).

Historically, open-weights models tend to be smaller (in number of total parameters), faster, and more cost-efficient; as such, the wider audience came to expect these models to be of "lower quality" or "light" versions of the higher-parameter frontier models (known as closed-weight models).

The difference between open-weights (or open-weight) models and closed weight models has nothing to do with the number of active parameters, overall cost, or efficiency. The distinction between the two relates to how users pay and/or interact with the models: open-source models are 1) free to access, as opposed to gated by subscriptions, 2) able to be trained and tuned (weights are "open" or able to be changed), as opposed to be the same for every user (weights are "closed"), and 3) give ultimate deployment flexibility, as it can be run on-prem, in the cloud, or through an API (either model creator's API, hosted service like AWS Bedrock, or self-hosted API; outlined in Exhibit 2).

Closed-weight models, alternately, can either be accessed directly from a model provider (the user pays a licensing fee, like a subscription, for access, and a token cost that serves as a proxy for GPU usage) or through a cloud provider should PII be a concern.

tweets.text:
The Yen carry trade is dying.

Before April 2025, the USD/JPY currency pair showed a close correlation with the 10Y rate differential between US and Japanese bonds.

This was driven by investors borrowing in Yen to fund higher-yielding US Dollar assets through the carry trade.

That relationship broke down after "Liberation Day," when trade war uncertainty triggered a surge in market volatility and forced investors to unwind some of their carry trade positions.

Meanwhile, the 10Y Treasury note yield is now trading ~2.0 percentage points above the Japanese 10Y Government Bond Yield, falling -1.0 percentage point since April 2025, near the lowest gap since 2021.

Yet, USD/JPY continued to move higher as the US Dollar strengthened against the Yen, despite the narrowing yield gap, breaking away from the interest rate differential that historically drove the pair.

In other words, the carry trade is losing its influence, with the Yen no longer driven primarily by rate differentials as investors increasingly price in Japan’s heavy debt burden and rising debt servicing costs.

Japan’s rising debt costs are becoming impossible to ignore.

tweets.text:
The relationship between stocks and bonds has completely flipped:

The 90-day correlation between the 10Y Treasury Yield and the S&P 500 is down to -0.48, its most negative reading since 1999.

This means that rising Treasury yields have recently been associated with weaker stock market performance, while falling yields have supported equities.

The current reading is even more negative than the 2022 bear market low of -0.42.

For context, before the 2020 pandemic, the correlation was positive for over a decade, with Treasury yields and equities often rising together as higher yields reflected stronger economic growth.

Currently, the negative correlation suggests investors are viewing higher yields less as a sign of economic strength and more as a result of inflation uncertainty and fiscal concerns.

All eyes are on the bond market.

"You're Always Looking Back" 🎵
(To the tune of "You're Always on My Mind")

I remember when the roads were quiet,
When every face looked just like mine.
Now every change feels like a warning,
So I call the old days "better times."

Don't build the roads I never traveled,
Don't teach the things I never learned.
I climbed the hill with yesterday's ladder—
Now pull it up once it's my turn.

Chorus

You're always looking backward,
Calling yesterday the best.
The ladder got you where you're standing,
Now nobody climbs the rest.

You're always looking backward,
Saying change has gone too far.
Funny how tomorrow ended
Right where you already are.

The future's knocking at the doorway,
But I pretend I can't hear the sound.
If I can't own tomorrow's story,
Then I'd rather shut the whole thing down.

I don't miss the past because it loved me,
I miss the comfort of the rules I knew.
It's easier to blame the new world rising
Than wonder if it simply outgrew you.

I call it tradition, call it common sense,
Wrap it all in stars and stripes.
But somewhere underneath the slogans
Lives the fear that I was right...

Final Chorus

You're always looking backward,
Calling yesterday the best.
The ladder got you where you're standing,
Now nobody climbs the rest.

I call it tradition, call it common sense,
Wrap it all in stars and stripes.
Ninety-three, I climbed the ladder.
Now I say it's gone too high.
Funny how it seemed much safer
Back when it was mine to climb."

Good Morning from #Latvia, where financially troubled airBaltic flew me in w/plenty of legroom and almost no hassle. Now I can only hope it flies me home too. Latvia owns 88%, Lufthansa 10%. What blew it up in March was fuel: airBaltic had hedged only about 10% of its 2026 jet fuel needs, so when the Iran war sent jet fuel flying, the entire cost base went w/it. Cash was €28m at 2025-year end against a €25m minimum liquidity covenant. No margin for anything.
The flag carrier's bond is a masterclass in what the word "secured" is actually worth. airBaltic sold €380m of 14.5% senior SECURED notes due 2029 at par in May 2024, at a whopping +1213bps over Bunds. They now trade at 40 cents today, yielding ~60%. Fitch has the airline at CCC- on Watch Negative and puts recovery at RR4, meaning holders get back 31% to 50% if it breaks. Back in December it was RR3. The collateral is shrinking faster than the debt.
The good assets are not in the pledge. The A220 fleet is leased, so the lessors hold the metal. What is left for bondholders is brand, spare parts, receivables and pledged accounts, all worth something only while the planes keep flying. The state owns 88% of the equity and guarantees exactly nothing.
On June 26 the airline skipped topping up the bond reserve account, which pushes the Aug 14 coupon to a 16.5% penalty rate. Monday's bondholder meeting was meant to fix things and failed on quorum. The rerun is Aug 17, 3 days after that coupon falls due, and by then the quorum threshold drops so low that a single bondholder can carry the vote. On the agenda: defer the next two coupons into the principal. The bailout is the risk: fresh capital would rank ahead of the old bonds, pushing today's "secured" holders one notch further back.
Lesson for yield hunters: "secured" tells you your rank in the queue. It tells you nothing about whether there is anything left when you get to the front.
